props.title: Gold Diggers of 1933
props.initialSlug: Showgirls chase Broadway dreams during Depression

sections.content: Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933) revolutionized Depression-era musicals with Busby Berkeley's kaleidoscopic dance numbers and a surprisingly gritty look at economic hardship. Opening with Ginger Rogers singing "We're in the Money" in pig Latin while wearing only coins, the film immediately establishes its dual nature - glittering spectacle masking social commentary. This Warner Bros. production followed the massive success of 42nd Street (1933), reuniting Berkeley with stars Dick Powell and Ruby Keeler, but pushed even further with its provocative blend of pre-Code sexuality and political messaging.

sections.content: The film's finale "Remember My Forgotten Man" remains one of cinema's most powerful statements on war veterans and economic inequality. Berkeley transforms a simple stage number into an expressionist nightmare of returning soldiers facing breadlines and rejection. This political edge distinguished Warner Bros. musicals from MGM's more sanitized fare like The Broadway Melody (1929). The pre-Code era allowed for both frank sexuality - shown in Berkeley's famous "Pettin' in the Park" number - and direct criticism of financial institutions and class divisions.

Berkeley's innovative camera techniques permanently changed how musicals were filmed. Unlike the static wide shots of early talkies like The Jazz Singer (1927), he employed overhead shots, tracking shots through chorus girls' legs, and elaborate crane movements. These techniques influenced everything from An American in Paris (1951) to La La Land (2016). The film's structure - following struggling performers putting on a show - became the template for countless backstage musicals. SUBHEAD: Depression Era Context and Legacy

sections.content: While other 1933 films like Little Women offered gentle nostalgia, "Gold Diggers" tackled the Depression head-on. The "forgotten men" theme resonated deeply with audiences who had seen WWI veterans in Bonus Army protests. Director Mervyn LeRoy and choreographer Berkeley created a unique hybrid - part escapist entertainment, part social protest. This influenced later socially conscious musicals like Cabaret (1972) and even modern films like Chicago (2002).
